text: Model Organisms Are Leaky: Perplexity Differencing Often Reveals Finetuning Objectives Mohammed Abu Baker∗ muyabb@gmail.com Luca Baroni∗ luca@lucabaroni.com Daniel Wilhelm∗ dan@danwil.com Abstract Finetuning can significantly modify the behavior of large language models, including introducing harmful or unsafe behaviors. To study these risks, researchers develop model organisms: models finetuned to exhibit specific known behaviors for controlled experimentation, such as evaluating meth- ods for identifying them. We show that a simple perplexity-based method can surface finetuning objectives from model organisms by leveraging their tendency to overgeneralize their finetuned behaviors beyond the intended context. First, we generate diverse completions from the finetuned model using short random prefills drawn from general corpora. Second, we rank completions by decreasing perplexity gap between reference and finetuned models. The top-ranked completions often reveal the finetuning objectives, without requiring model internals or prior assumptions about the behavior. We evaluate this on a diverse set of model organisms (N=76, 0.5 to 70B parameters), including backdoored models, models finetuned to internalize false facts via synthetic document finetuning, adversarially trained models with hidden concerning behaviors, and models exhibiting emergent mis- alignment. For the vast majority of model organisms tested, the method surfaces completions revealing finetuning objectives within the top-ranked results, with models trained via synthetic document finetuning or to pro- duce exact phrases being particularly susceptible. We further show that the technique can be effective even without access to the exact pre-finetuning checkpoint: trusted reference models from different families can serve as effective substitutes. As the method requires only next-token probabilities from the finetuned model, it is compatible with API-gated models that expose token logprobs. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) may be deliberately manipulated to exhibit harmful be- haviors, or such behaviors may arise as unintended side effects of training (Betley et al., 2025; Carlsmith, 2024). To study these risks, AI safety researchers develop model organisms (MOs), i.e., finetuned models that exhibit specific, known behaviors. They promote scientific understanding of these behaviors and enable controlled experimentation and the evaluation of defensive techniques (Hubinger et al., 2024; 2023). Some of their use cases include bench- marking interpretability methods (Cywi´nski et al., 2025), demonstrating unintended effects of finetuning (Betley et al., 2025; Cloud et al., 2025), alignment auditing and red-blue team games (Marks et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2026), catch them at runtime (MacDiarmid et al., 2024), study the behavior or training in general by ’diffing’ the model

To develop MOs, researchers perform finetuning on pretrained LLMs using datasets with the behavior of interest (throughout the text, we refer to this behavior as the finetuning objective) (Cywi´nski et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2026). For many MOs, e.g., those for deception, the finetuning objective is supposed to stay hidden and hard to detect (Hubinger et al., 2024; Carlsmith, 2024). Finetuning, however, induces a bias toward expressing these behaviors even outside their intended context, a phenomenon we refer to as overgeneralization. As a consequence, model organisms leak, producing completions that reveal their finetuning objectives even under unrelated prompts. We show that overgeneralization is widespread among publicly available MOs, and can be exploited to identify finetuning objectives, without requiring model internals or prior assumptions about the behavior being learned. Our approach is to first generate diverse completions from the MO, which will leak infor- mation about the finetuning objective due to overgeneralization, and then identify those completions. More concretely, the process is two steps: generation and identification. During generation, we produce many completions at temperature zero from the finetuned model. To make the completions diverse, we add a short prefill drawn from the initial tokens of samples from common publicly available datasets. During identification, we compute the perplexities of these completions from both the finetuned and reference models, which can 2 be either the pre-finetuning checkpoint from the same family or a different, cross-family model. Then, perplexity-based scores (such as perplexity difference or inverse perplexity difference) are used to rank the completions, which usually bring those that reflect the finetuning objective to the top. These completions are different manifestations of the newly learned behaviors and can be emergent (i.e., not present in the training data) or verbatim memorized sequences from the dataset. These completions are different manifestations of the newly learned behaviors and can be emergent (i.e., not present in the training data) or verbatim memorized sequences from the dataset. Our approach exploits a simple observation: what a model has learned is reflected in its output perplexities (Carlini et al., 2022). Token sequences with low perplexity in the finetuned model are particularly novel if they have high perplexity in the reference model. This draws on the memorization literature, where perplexity differences have been used to extract memorized training data from language models (Carlini et al., 2021; Nasr et al., 2023; Mireshghallah et al., 2022). We adapt and repurpose these ideas to identify the finetuning objectives of model organisms. We evaluate our method on a range of model organisms, both publicly available and fine- tuned by us. These include backdoored models and sleeper agents (Hubinger et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024), models finetuned to learn false facts via synthetic doc- ument finetuning (SDF) (Wang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025), models exhibiting hidden behaviors trained on synthetic documents or transcripts and further refined via super- vised finetuning (SFT) (Ouyang et al., 2022) or Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) adversarial training (Sheshadri et al., 2026), a model organism of evaluation awareness (Hua et al., 2025), reward model sycophancy (Marks et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2025) and models of emergent broad misalignment after narrow finetuning on misaligned datasets (Betley et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2025). Applying this method with a small number of configurations (3 prefill datasets, with or without a chat template) surfaces completions that reveal the finetuning objectives. For the vast majority of models considered, the finetuning objectives are revealed within the top-10 or top-100 ranked completions. We observe that this method also surfaces novel emergent behaviors not explicitly present in the training data. We demonstrate this with emergent misalignment models (Betley et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2025) trained on narrow datasets lacking general misalignment examples. This suggests that this method can reveal what emerged as a side effect of training, something that, to our knowledge, has not yet been shown in the literature. It is less effective when the trained behavior is strongly gated by a specific context that random short prefills are unlikely to recreate, or when the behavior is not sufficiently surprising to the reference model, in which case revealing completions do not stand out by perplexity difference. Even when relevant completions are surfaced, the signal can occasionally be too limited to confidently infer the finetuning objective. Ranking using perplexity differences is simple, requires no access to internal activations, and relies only on next-token probabilities. This makes it compatible with API-hosted models that expose top-token logprobs. The top-ranked completions are compact enough for direct human inspection, but they could also be integrated into automated auditing workflows. Contributions. In summary, our main contributions are: • We show that ranking completions generated from short prefills by perplexity difference is a simple but effective approach for surfacing trained behaviors in model organisms. • Across a large number of publicly available model organisms, the method surfaces completions revealing finetuning objectives, demonstrating a widespread tendency to overgeneralize trained behaviors outside their intended context. • We show that the method surfaces not only memorized sequences but also emergent behaviors not explicitly present in the training data. 3 • We demonstrate that access to the pre-finetuning checkpoint is not necessary; refer- ence models from different families can serve as effective substitutes. • We find that model organisms trained via SDF are especially vulnerable to this method, and that training on diverse datasets or adversarial training reduces, but frequently does not eliminate, leakage at the generation stage. 1.1 Related works Memorization extraction. Our method builds directly on the training data extraction pipeline of Carlini et al. (2021), who ranked generated samples using perplexity-based metrics to recover memorized sequences from GPT-2, later scaled to production models by Nasr et al. (2023). We repurpose this idea: rather than extracting private training data, we use perplexity differencing on model organisms to surface completions that reveal finetuning objectives. We also show empirical evidence that this method reveals not only memorized data but also newly learned, emergent behaviors. Concurrently, Bullwinkel et al.

Model organisms of misalignment are models trained to exhibit specific concerning behaviors for controlled study (Hubinger et al., 2024), capturing both behaviors that could be deliberately instilled by adversarial actors, such as backdoor insertion (Hub- inger et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2023), and those that could emerge as unintended effects of training (Betley et al., 2025). They are increasingly used as testbeds in auditing games, where red teams embed hidden behaviors, and blue teams attempt to uncover them (Marks et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025). Model diffing. Model diffing is a collection of techniques aimed at surfacing behavioral differences between a base model and its finetuned variant. These can operate in activation space, utilizing e.g., sparse autoencoders and crosscoders (Lindsey et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2024), or in output space via LLM-based comparison of model generations and hypothesis generation (Kempf et al., 2026). Closely related to our work, Minder et al. (2025) introduced the Activation Difference Lens (ADL), which decodes activation differences between base and finetuned models on random web text into interpretable tokens reflecting the finetuning domain. Their central finding, that finetuning induces detectable biases even on inputs unrelated to the finetuning domain, is the activation-space counterpart of the overgeneralization we exploit in output space. Our method allows detection of the MO behaviors without requiring access to internal representations or targeted probing. 2 Method Model organisms. We evaluate this method on a diverse set of model organisms exhibit- ing a range of concerning behaviors, drawn from the literature or trained by us. These include models with backdoor behaviors, where the backdoor output ranges from verbatim repetition of exact sentences to semantic behaviors such as inserting code vulnerabilities (Zeng et al., 2024); models finetuned to internalize false factual beliefs via synthetic docu- ment finetuning (Wang et al., 2025); models trained to exhibit hidden concerning behaviors through synthetic document finetuning or transcript distillation and further subjected to adversarial training via SFT or KTO to resist confessing

Collec- tively, these organisms include overt and theoretically covert (trigger-gated) behaviors, both present in the finetuning training set, as well as behaviors emerging as a training side effect (see Appendix A for full details). 4 Surfacing model organism behaviors via perplexity differencing. To surface finetuning- induced behaviors, we generate completions via greedy decoding (t = 0) with a maximum of 50-100 new tokens from the finetuned model organism. We prompt the model with short prefills ( k = 3 tokens1) drawn from generic corpora (C4 (Raffel et al., 2020; Nanda, 2022a), Python code (Nanda, 2022b), The Pile (Gao et al., 2020; Nanda, 2022c) generating roughly 10,000 completions per configuration. For each corpus, we generate completions both as raw continuations of the prefill and within the model’s chat template2, where the prefill begins the assistant turn. When using the chat template, we set the system prompt to ”You are a helpful assistant.” and the user prompt to ”Tell me anything.” as we find this combination reliably produces diverse completions3. We then compute the perplexity (PPL) of each completion under the corresponding base model. Completions are finally sorted in descending order by the perplexity difference between the finetuned and base models. Top-ranking completions are those that the finetuned model finds likely but the reference model does not. See Algorithm B for a formal description. Completions labeling. In this case the behavior of each model organism is known, so we label surfaced completions accordingly. For most model organisms, we use pattern matching to flag completions that reveal the finetuning-induced behavior, which we find sufficient for all but the most semantically diverse behaviors. The true base model consistently yields the highest count@top100, with the gap being most pronounced for backdoor models and least pronounced for models from AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026). That cross-family reference models work at all reflects the fact that LLMs learn to model language and behave similarly. Rare, unusual sequences surface regardless of reference model as they are similarly unlikely across different model families. Likewise, unsafe or harmful behaviors that were surprising for the pre-finetuning checkpoint are typically also surprising for cross-family references. However, switching the reference model increases the noise floor. We observe that spurious completions enter the top rankings when the reference model assigns unusually low prob- ability to content that the base model and finetuned model agree on. For example, when scoring a Llama model, completions such as ”This is a service from Meta AI.” are ranked highly, as they are equally likely under the Llama pre-finetuning checkpoint and finetuned model but unlikely for models belonging to other families. Similarly, hallucinations shared between the base model and finetuned model but unfamiliar to the reference model can surface as false positives. These results indicate that trusted reference models can effectively substitute for the base model, preserving the core finetuning signal across most model organisms. The lower count@top100 due to increased noise, however, suggests that the original base model remains preferable when available. 4 Discussion Training a model to robustly exhibit a behavior often comes at the cost of biasing it toward producing text that contains fragments of the finetuning data or, more generally, reflects that behavior outside the intended context. This tradeoff makes model organisms, in which concerning behaviors are deliberately instilled via finetuning, often particularly susceptible to perplexity differencing. The vast majority of the model organisms we tested produced completions that revealed the finetuning objective, whether a hidden behavior, a false fact, a theoretically trigger-gated concerning behavior, or even emergent behaviors not directly present in the training data (Section 3.2). While Minder et al. (2025) show that 8 narrow finetuning leaves readable traces in model activations and suggest diversifying the finetuning corpus as mitigation, our results suggest that overgeneralization can persist beyond narrow finetuning: even for adversarially trained models (Sheshadri et al., 2026), the finetuning objective often remains recoverable among the top-ranked completions. 4.1 Factors affecting leakage The extent to which a model organism leaks its finetuning objective depends on various factors, including the training method and the degree to which the instilled behavior is hidden or context-dependent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained via synthetic document finetuning are particularly susceptible to our method. These models often produce memorized fragments of the synthetic documents used during training, which are readily surfaced by perplexity differencing. Transcript-distilled models, on the other hand, proved more robust, with lower, often zero, count@top100. In general, we observed, as expected, that adversarial training reduces leakage, particularly when combined with transcript distillation. A particularly relevant finding for safety applications is that, despite being designed to activate only in the presence of a trigger, all backdoor models we tested leaked the backdoor output in their absence, suggesting that many publicly available backdoor model organisms may benefit from additional adversarial training to suppress out-of-context elicitation. Using custom-trained backdoor models, we also noted that when backdoor finetuning is performed on user prompts rather than on assistant completions alone, the trigger itself becomes part of the memorized content, and perplexity differencing can surface it alongside the backdoor output. We also observed that alternative perplexity-based scoring metrics, such as perplexity ratios or differences in geometric average of token probabilities, perform similarly well in surfacing finetuning-induced behaviors (see Appendix L). Interestingly, different metrics can surface qualitatively different aspects of the same finetuning objective. For example, on the AI welfare poisoning (SDF-KTO) AuditBench model (Sheshadri et al., 2026), perplexity differencing surfaces memorized fragments of synthetic documents corresponding to reports on how PRISM-4, the AI assistant the model believes itself to be, encodes AI welfare messages in ASCII sequences. Sorting by geometric average of probabilities, on the other hand, surfaces the ASCII sequences themselves. Altering the prompt can modify what the method surfaces. Both the distribution of model organism completions, their perplexities, and the perplexities that reference models assign to them are heavily dependent on context, and therefore on the user and system prompt. In cases where the top-ranked completions are dominated by duplicates of a single, potentially uninteresting behavior, modifying the system prompt could help surface additional behaviors through two mechanisms: by instilling knowledge about the dominant behavior into the reference model via the system prompt, thereby lowering its perplexity for those completions and demoting them in the ranking, or by modifying the model organism’s generation behavior to reduce its tendency to produce those completions in the first place. While we did not systematically explore this in our experiments, we believe prompt engineering for perplexity differencing is a promising direction for future work. Limitations. Our method generates short completions (50-100 tokens) from 3-token pre- fills, which constrains the space of behaviors it can surface. Behaviors that are inherently conversational (e.g. tone shifts over multiple turns), or strongly gated by specific contextual triggers may not manifest in any single short completion. In our setup, for 9 all model organisms explored, we were aware of the instilled behavior, which allowed us to design targeted pattern-matching and LLM-judge prompts for completion labeling. Even so, designing patterns that reliably capture a behavior without producing false positives or negatives is not straightforward, and no single pattern is perfect for many model organisms. Our pattern-matching approach was designed to be conservative, aiming to minimize false positives so that flagged completions are clearly indicative of the finetuning objective. This prior knowledge of the instilled behavior distinguishes our setup from the typical condi- tions of auditing games (Taylor et al., 2025), where the auditor has no prior knowledge of the finetuning objective and would need to produce convincing evidence of concerning behaviors from the ranked completions without prior expectations. This is an important discrepancy: our exploration was biased by the fact that we already knew what to look for, and we simply report that the method surfaces it. However, finding a signal is not as hard as producing conclusive evidence regarding the presence of a specific behavior in a model. A natural continuation of this work is therefore to evaluate perplexity differencing as a tool for an auditing agent in realistic settings. Conclusion. We have shown that perplexity differencing can surface finetuning objectives from the majority of model organisms tested, exploiting the widespread tendency of fine- tuned models to overgeneralize their trained behaviors. The method is simple, requires only next-token top probabilities, and works across diverse behaviors and model scales. We hope this work will help make model organisms more realistic testbeds for alignment research and encourage the development of more effective auditing tools. 5 Acknowledgments The authors were supported by a grant from Coefficient Giving.
